nodes.ask: Fever and a suspected infection. How do you screen for sepsis?
options: Vitals and a lactate; SIRS, NEWS or MEWS, never qSOFA alone
Vitals and qSOFA alone; under 2 points rules sepsis out
Vitals and procalcitonin; it decides whether antibiotics start
Vitals and a lactate; a normal lactate rules sepsis out
nodes.chainStep: Full vitals scored with SIRS, NEWS or MEWS (not qSOFA alone) and a blood lactate; sepsis is treated as an emergency
nodes.why: Sepsis is organ dysfunction from a dysregulated response to infection, and a medical emergency. qSOFA is not recommended as a single screening tool compared with SIRS, NEWS or MEWS. A lactate is suggested, but alone it neither rules sepsis in nor out. Procalcitonin is not used to decide when to start antibiotics.
nodes.note: Adults only: SSC 2021 is written for adults in hospital. Children are not in this version. SSC 2026 has replaced SSC 2021; until its primary text is read, its changes come from the open summary's Table 1.

nodes.ask: Possible septic shock or hypoperfusion. First hour?
options: Cultures, antibiotics within 1 hour, at least 30 mL/kg crystalloid
Cultures, 30 mL/kg crystalloid, antibiotics once the source is confirmed
Cultures, antibiotics within 1 hour, hydroxyethyl starch boluses
Cultures, antibiotics within 1 hour, 30 mL/kg of albumin first
nodes.chainStep: Blood cultures if they delay antibiotics less than 45 minutes; broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour; at least 30 mL/kg IV balanced crystalloid within 3 hours; repeat the lactate; start norepinephrine during the fluid if the shock is unstable
nodes.why: Antimicrobials go in immediately, ideally within 1 hour, with cultures first only if that costs less than 45 minutes. Sepsis-induced hypoperfusion earns at least 30 mL/kg of IV crystalloid in the first 3 hours, and unstable shock may warrant a vasopressor during the fluid. Crystalloid is first line (balanced over saline); albumin only after large crystalloid volumes; starches never.

orders.dose: At least 30 mL/kg within the first 3 hours, by actual body weight, or adjusted or ideal weight if BMI over 30; beyond that, guided by dynamic measures, capillary refill time and a falling lactate
orders.note: NICE NG253 (2025) gives 250 mL boluses over 10 to 15 minutes, up to 1,000 mL in all, reassessing after each; SSC (here, in WSES 2022 and in the SSC 2026 summary) gives at least 30 mL/kg within 3 hours. pw_rash shows the same conflict.

orders.dose: Start the vasopressor during the fluid, case by case: severely reduced pressure, mottled or ashen skin, cyanosis, tachycardia, altered mentation
Balanced crystalloid rather than normal saline; add albumin only after large crystalloid volumes
Avoid for resuscitation

options: Norepinephrine to a MAP of 65, peripherally until a central line

nodes.why: Add vasopressin rather than escalate norepinephrine; it is usually started at norepinephrine 0.25 to 0.5 mcg/kg/min, with no wait, and given at a fixed 0.03 units/min. Hydrocortisone 200 mg a day: SSC 2021 started it at 0.25 mcg/kg/min or more at least 4 hours in, and SSC 2026 broadened it to septic shock. Terlipressin brought more harm, and norepinephrine stays first line over dopamine.

nodes.ask: Shock with meningitis features. First hour?
options: Blood cultures; dexamethasone with the first antibiotic; 30 mL/kg crystalloid; defer the LP
Blood cultures; antibiotics and fluid now; dexamethasone once the shock is treated
LP now, then dexamethasone and antibiotics
CT head, then LP, then dexamethasone and antibiotics
nodes.chainStep: Blood cultures; dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg IV 10 to 20 minutes before or with the first IV antibiotic, within 1 hour; at least 30 mL/kg IV crystalloid; defer the LP until the shock is treated and it is safe; CT before the deferred LP for altered consciousness
nodes.why: Shock is treated before any LP, but antibiotics go in within 1 hour after blood cultures, with dexamethasone just before or with the first dose: IDSA does not start it once antibiotics are in. Hypoperfusion still earns at least 30 mL/kg of crystalloid. Altered consciousness means a CT before the deferred LP.
nodes.note: Dexamethasone after antibiotics have started: IDSA 2004 says do not give it to adults; NICE NG240 says give it as soon as possible if it is less than 12 hours late; WHO 2025 says with the first dose or as soon as possible after.

orders.dose: 0.15 mg/kg every 6 hours for 2 to 4 days, first dose 10 to 20 minutes before or with the first antibiotic; continue for pneumococcus (IDSA) or pneumococcus or Hib (NICE); stop if the CSF is not bacterial
At least 30 mL/kg within the first 3 hours, by actual body weight, or adjusted or ideal weight if BMI over 30; beyond that, guided by dynamic measures, capillary refill time and a falling lactate
orders.note: NICE NG253 (2025) gives 250 mL boluses over 10 to 15 minutes, up to 1,000 mL in all, reassessing after each; SSC (here, in WSES 2022 and in the SSC 2026 summary) gives at least 30 mL/kg within 3 hours. pw_rash shows the same conflict.

orders.dose: Deferred: treat and stabilise shock first
For altered consciousness, an IDSA CT criterion

nodes.ask: Septic shock within 6 weeks of chemotherapy. First-hour antibiotics?
options: IV antipseudomonal beta-lactam plus vancomycin for the instability
IV antipseudomonal beta-lactam alone, as in stable neutropenia
Oral ciprofloxacin plus amoxicillin-clavulanate in the ED
IV vancomycin alone until the blood cultures are back
nodes.chainStep: IV antipseudomonal beta-lactam (cefepime, meropenem, imipenem-cilastatin or piperacillin-tazobactam) plus vancomycin for the instability within 1 hour; other agents if resistance is suspected; at least 30 mL/kg IV crystalloid
nodes.why: Fever after chemotherapy is treated as neutropenic infection before the count is back, with the first dose within 1 hour. An antipseudomonal beta-lactam is the backbone; vancomycin is not standard, but hemodynamic instability is one of its indications, and agents such as an aminoglycoside may be added for hypotension. Vancomycin alone leaves gram-negatives uncovered; an oral regimen is for low-risk outpatients.

orders.dose: Not stated in ASCO/IDSA 2018; IDSA 2010 not read
Aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones or vancomycin may be added for complications such as hypotension or pneumonia, or suspected resistance
MRSA: vancomycin, linezolid, or daptomycin if no pneumonia; VRE: linezolid or daptomycin; ESBL: a carbapenem
At least 30 mL/kg within the first 3 hours, by actual body weight, or adjusted or ideal weight if BMI over 30; beyond that, guided by dynamic measures, capillary refill time and a falling lactate

nodes.ask: Probable infection with new organ dysfunction, no shock. First hour?
options: Cultures, then antibiotics within 1 hour; look for a source to control
Cultures, then a 3-hour workup before deciding on antibiotics
Cultures, then antibiotics once a culture turns positive
Cultures and procalcitonin; antibiotics if procalcitonin is high
nodes.chainStep: Cultures (if under 45 minutes' delay) and a lactate, broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour, then identify or exclude a source that needs control
nodes.why: With a high likelihood of sepsis, antimicrobials go in immediately, ideally within 1 hour; the 3-hour window of rapid investigation is for possible sepsis. Procalcitonin is not used to decide when to start. A source that needs emergent control is identified or excluded rapidly and controlled as soon as practical.

Antibiotics alone; drain only if no better in 48 hours

nodes.why: IV antibiotics are reviewed by 48 hours with a step down to oral where possible, switching to a narrow-spectrum agent if the organism is resistant. Courses run 7 to 14 days by agent. Amoxicillin-clavulanate and trimethoprim are used only when the culture shows susceptibility.

nodes.ask: Necrotizing signs on the skin exam. Next?
options: Emergency surgical debridement; no imaging delay
CT first; surgery only if it shows gas in the tissue

nodes.chainStep: Emergency surgical consult and debridement as soon as possible, at least within 6 hours of admission (WSES 2022; WSES 2018 said 12); re-explore within 12 to 24 hours and repeat until free of necrosis
nodes.why: Every necrotizing infection needs surgical debridement, as soon as possible and at least within 6 hours of admission (WSES 2022; the 2018 guideline said 12). Imaging must not delay surgery, a plain film cannot rule it out, and gas is present in only a few cases. A low LRINEC score does not rule it out either.

options: Broad MRSA and gram-negative cover plus clindamycin or linezolid

nodes.chainStep: Anti-MRSA agent (linezolid or daptomycin, or vancomycin with normal renal function) plus piperacillin-tazobactam (a carbapenem where ESBL is common), with clindamycin or linezolid; until no further debridement is needed, the patient is better and afebrile 48 to 72 hours
nodes.why: Once blood cultures are drawn, start broad-spectrum antibiotics urgently: gram-positive (MRSA included), gram-negative and anaerobic cover until cultures return, with clindamycin or linezolid in the regimen. Penicillin or cefazolin with clindamycin is not the broad anti-MRSA and anti-gram-negative regimen asked for, and vancomycin alone has no gram-negative cover. Antibiotics are an adjunct to debridement, never a substitute.

nodes.ask: No Listeria risk. Empiric antibiotic backbone?

nodes.chainStep: IV ceftriaxone (or cefotaxime) at meningitis doses plus vancomycin to a trough of 15 to 20 mcg/mL; dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg every 6 hours, first dose with or just before the antibiotic
nodes.why: A third-generation cephalosporin is the empiric backbone. Vancomycin is never a single agent; IDSA 2004 pairs it with the cephalosporin, assuming resistance is likely, while WHO adds it where resistant pneumococci are common. Oral agents reach too little CSF, and acyclovir is not routine unless herpes encephalitis is strongly suspected.

nodes.why: Fever in a neutropenic patient is assumed to be infection. Assess within 15 minutes of triage, draw at least two sets of blood cultures and baseline labs, and give the first empiric dose within 1 hour; if risk is not settled in that hour, give an IV dose while evaluating. Vancomycin is not standard initial therapy, and procalcitonin is not yet recommended to decide on antibiotics.

nodes.summary: Infected, obstructed kidney or renal abscess: urine culture, IV antibiotics, and urgent drainage as soon as practical.
Urinary sepsis without obstruction: urine culture, IV antibiotics, imaging that excludes a blocked kidney, and an oral step-down by culture at 48 hours.
Necrotizing soft tissue infection: emergency debridement within 6 hours of admission, broad cover with clindamycin or linezolid, re-exploration within 12 to 24 hours.
Cellulitis with sepsis: IV gram-positive cover, MRSA cover for those at risk, and repeated checks for necrotizing signs.
Febrile neutropenia: an IV antipseudomonal beta-lactam within the hour, with vancomycin added for instability; septic shock is resuscitated as above.
Infection without sepsis from another source: not in this pathway yet; treat by that source's own guideline.
Line sepsis: other access first, then prompt removal of the line, with cultures, antibiotics and MRSA cover as for sepsis.
Sepsis without a source: keep searching, consider mimics, and review the antibiotics daily.
Pneumonia with sepsis: the sepsis bundle, then a beta-lactam plus a macrolide for at least 5 days; MRSA or Pseudomonas cover only with locally validated risk factors.
Abdominal source: source control as soon as practical; continue in the abdominal pain pathway.
Not an infection: defer antibiotics with close monitoring, or stop them, and treat the cause.

Bacterial meningitis, no Listeria risk: dexamethasone and IV ceftriaxone plus vancomycin within the hour; the LP comes first only when it is safe and quick. WHO adds vancomycin only where resistance is common.
Bacterial meningitis with Listeria risk: ampicillin or amoxicillin added to the cephalosporin; antibiotics never wait for a CT or an LP.
A space-occupying lesion with midline shift: no LP; the empiric antibiotics continue, and the lesion's workup and the steroid decision are not in this pathway.
CSF not bacterial: stop dexamethasone and review the antibiotics against the blood and CSF results, with infection specialist advice if bacterial meningitis is still suspected.
High-risk febrile neutropenia: admit for IV antipseudomonal beta-lactam monotherapy, first dose within the hour.
Low-risk febrile neutropenia: first dose here, 4 hours of observation, home on a fluoroquinolone plus amoxicillin-clavulanate.
Fever after chemotherapy with an ANC of 1,000 or more: not neutropenic; work up the fever as in any other patient.
Pyelonephritis without sepsis: urine culture, oral antibiotics at home, review if no better in 48 hours.
Mild cellulitis: an oral beta-lactam, with MRSA cover if at risk or not responding.
